37 The battery of a car has an internal resistance of 0.10 Ω and an electromotive force of 12 V. When
the battery is connected to the starter motor, the potential difference across the battery terminals
is 7.0 V.
What is the current supplied to the starter motor?
A
50 A
B
70 A
C
120 A
D
190 A

hints: Notice the two voltages are different: e.m.f. $12 \text{ V}$ and terminal p.d. $7.0 \text{ V}$ with internal resistance $0.10 \, \Omega$.
Recall that terminal p.d. is less than e.m.f. by the voltage lost across internal resistance: $V = E - Ir$.
Calculate the lost volts $E - V$ first, then divide that $5.0 \text{ V}$ drop by $0.10 \, \Omega$ to get the current in $\text{A}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: $E = 12 \text{ V}$, $r = 0.10 \, \Omega$ and terminal p.d. $V = 7.0 \text{ V}$ when supplying the starter motor.
State the governing relation for a source with internal resistance: $V = E - Ir$, where $Ir$ is the lost volts inside the battery.
Rearrange for current: $Ir = E - V$, so $I = (E - V)/r$.
Calculate and check units: $I = 50 \text{ A}$, a large but sensible starter-motor current.

A.explanation: Current gives lost volts of $12 - 7.0 = 5.0 \text{ V}$ across $0.10 \, \Omega$, so $I = 5.0/0.10 = 50 \text{ A}$.

B.explanation: This divides only the terminal p.d. by $r$, $7.0/0.10 = 70 \text{ A}$, ignoring that $r$ carries the lost volts $E-V$, not $V$.

C.explanation: This divides the full e.m.f. by $r$, $12/0.10 = 120 \text{ A}$, which would be the short-circuit current when $V = 0$.

D.explanation: This adds e.m.f. and terminal p.d., $(12+7.0)/0.10 = 190 \text{ A}$, instead of subtracting to find the voltage lost inside the battery.
